Tupak Abu Hanjour (born 18 September 1961) is a German scholar and writer of Islamic studies who works in Hamas, currently one of the top religious leaders in the Palestinian Authority. A board member of the World Association of Islamic Trusts, he is the president of the Association for Jewish and Islamic Heritage of New York.

Life
Abu Hanjour was born in Sorido, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, where he spent his childhood and adolescence. He lived and studied in Saudi Arabia, attended high school in Sweden, one of the foreign universities of the time.

His grandfather, Halman Samir Abu Hanjour, had served as a political prisoner in the Red Sea settlement of Panjshir, and had taught under Imam Muhammad Khasawneh in Jerusalem, and the Imam Muhammad Hassan al-Tamimiyeh of Shejaiya, from which Hanjour's father Nu'on Shehadeh originated.

He studied Islamic philosophy in Geneva, at the Free University and the Institut Suisse de Theologie et Philosophie. He also studied Islamic Jurisprudence in the College of Advocates of Stuttgart, Leipzig and Riyadh.

Abu Hanjour has published over a dozen books and articles primarily on the lives and activities of the great scholars. Abscisic acid (ABA) is the principal signal for seed development in plant. It is synthesized via a series of biosynthetic processes. One process is the biosynthesis of jasmonic acid (JA), which can be catalyzed by enzyme MYC2 that specifically regulates the ABA receptor SnRK2. SnRK2 is a unique multi-protein complexes that can activate ABA-activated ABA response genes defined as MeJA-responsive genes, which regulate the jasmonate-insensitive GA-response genes defined as gibberellin group-A/B-responsive genes. In addition, SnRK2 also activates JA-responsive geneDEF4 which is either induced by 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC)-dependent genes to negatively regulate ACC-dependent genes via antagonism with ABFs and bHLHs. The research findings show co-dependent regulation between SnRK2, DEF** and JA-RESONANT GENES which are involved in ABA signaling tumorigenesis signaling. Furthermore, some of them have homologous and/or syntenic with the ABA-INSENSITIVE DEAR (AID) gene family. The Besnoi JA-insensitive plant 2 (BAP2) Knma1 and associated genes are considered to play a most important role in this process. We reviewed the medical records of 12 patients who had 668 CD4 counts less than or equal to 300 CD4 cells/mm3 and whose HIV-1 viral loads had been less than or equal to 20,000 copies/mL and of whom five had CD4 counts of less than 100 cells/mm3 at the beginning of treatment; these patients constitute the high-risk group. All of the 10 patients infected with HIV-1 had a fulminant type of Tuberculosis. Eight of 10 had been treated with antiretroviral therapy but two were virologically suppressed (median CD4 less than or equal to 50 cells/mm3); one of them died of tuberculosis, another had evolved dilated cardiomyopathy and died of infections mainly HIV-associated, and the third received anthropomimetic drugs and died of HIV infection. The eight patients in whom we have had follow-up and all the new infections they had evolved after treatment were all B-cell lymphomas; these patients constitute the splenectomized-B-cell type, which may be a variant of Reed-Sternberg's B cell lymphoma. The other two patients, the 29 and 34-year-old brothers, did not die of HIV infection; one of them died of a complication of HIV infection and with tuberculosis and the other had lymphoma and survived for a long time without AIDS. The third patient had a myopathy that was known to be due to a viralic reaction. The patients constitute a group of high-risk patients in which HIV-1 virus loads should be monitored with the combination of CD4 cell counts and viral loads in order to prevent development of fatal immunodeficiency. <|endoftext|>Comment on 'Becoming what you are': social behavior affecting behavior in biomedical mastering courses'

Abstract

Several studies since the 1980s have demonstrated that individuals usually change what they teach, such that the most important lessons are learned from students who are either influenced more by peers than previous teachers (§12.3.1) or who are generally more innovative and able to communicate their understanding with others (§1.3.3). This tendency of students to demonstrate a wider range of changes of types and engagements across topics indicates that students may be developing a more comprehensive understanding of the textbook than the one they learn and disseminate to their teachers. In these courses, however, students tend to critically appraise the practice of teachers rather than just teacher behavior. Knowing more about students’ experiences and interests allows us to pinpoint possible paths toward uncovering the causes of failure or improvement in important course topics, for instance, when teachers end up using predefined sets of exercises, but not when students make the effort to innovate on Earth Science, in a way that has no known tryout of its own. For an effective interaction with teachers, some aspect has to be changed in the school environment. Such changes include the kind of formative feedback given to students using forms that students had to fill out for the assignment (here, we assumed that teachers who update topics during class presentations would be more satisfied with students’ student feedback); the kind of feedback provided to student-teachers by administrators and faculty (the current feedback that allows student comments to modulate teacher behavior, although not always appropriately) and the kind of feedback provided to students about their learning progress and specific challenges and opportunities (particularly the kind that encourages students to use student-constructs for action, rather than pushing them to produce more or longer versions of parts of final concepts). To better understand who students are and whom to deal with, we experimented with a multimedia workshop by a didactic course rather than by the didactic course itself. Our results suggest that while different teachers of biomedicine may act differently in implementing the WU-BMC model, policies developed in one type of school context may not be directly transferable to another.<|endoftext|>Depressive symptoms and corresponding increases in cocaine relapse rates: an investigation of the meaning of drug use to the individual.

Time-reversal symmetry breaking effects occur in many optoelectronic devices because of either the symmetry breaking or the broken symmetry. In this work, we report time-reversal symmetry breaking effects in the transport properties of quantum wires through an anisotropic multicomponent quantum wire. The zero-bias conductance shows non-monotonic and asymmetric behaviors as a function of the strength of the external magnetic field and is dependent on the direction of the applied magnetic field.
